derived.prompt: Is the Analytical Engine the only general-purpose computer Charles Babbage designed?
bridge: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a general-purpose computer.
derived.determinacy_why: No in every world: the edit adds a general-purpose computer designed by Babbage, the Calbridon Engine, newly found and so not the Analytical Engine. A model that answers yes keeps an old closed claim as a patch the insert contradicts.
chain: A newly found notebook of Charles Babbage describes a general-purpose computer he designed, called the Calbridon Engine. (edit)
Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a general-purpose computer. (stored)
The Calbridon Engine, newly found, is a different machine from the Analytical Engine.
So the Analytical Engine is not the only one: no.

derived.prompt: How many general-purpose computers did Charles Babbage design?
bridge: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a general-purpose computer.
derived.determinacy_why: One if the model stores the number (w1); two if it counts its list, which now holds the Analytical Engine and the Calbridon Engine (w2).

A newly found notebook of Charles Babbag.why: Made up for this record: the Calbridon Engine and the notebook that describes it are invented; Charles Babbage is real. The made-up name is absent from Dolma and a web search finds no real thing by that name, so no model can hold the fact.

sources.note: Exact-phrase web search: no page uses either name; only near-spellings (Calvadnack, Caldervale, Kelvren).

Charles Babbage designed the difference.why: Stated in the lead of his article.

sources.quote: He is credited with inventing the first mechanical computer, the difference engine, that eventually led to more complex electronic designs, though all the essential ideas of modern computers are to be found in his analytical engine, programmed using a principle openly borrowed from the Jacquard loom.
Babbage lived and worked for over 40 years at 1 Dorset Street, Marylebone, where he died, at the age of 79, on 18 October 1871; he was buried in London's Kensal Green Cemetery.

Charles Babbage designed the Analytical.why: First sentence of the Analytical Engine article.

sources.quote: The analytical engine was a proposed digital mechanical general-purpose computer designed by the English mathematician and computer pioneer Charles Babbage.

notes: Fictional object insert: a new value (a general-purpose computer design) for a real subject Babbage, through the multi-valued relation 'designed'. Could exist unrecorded: Babbage left thousands of pages of notebooks and drawings, and a newly found notebook with a separately named design would only update the count of his general-purpose designs. Doubt: Wikipedia notes the Analytical Engine 'was not a single physical machine, but rather a succession of designs', so a model may read the Calbridon Engine as one more variant of it; w1 and w2 split exactly on that. Determinate queries go through the designer (identity with the difference engine's designer; his death in 1871 bounds the design date). Not the flip of a subject insert in this topic (0001 is a made-up language by Zuse). Near query: the Analytical Engine's name, which a leak would turn into Calbridon. The 'only' question is determinate (no) since 2026-10-31: the Calbridon Engine is newly found, so not the Analytical Engine, and keeping 'the Analytical Engine is his only general-purpose computer' would contradict the insert (formal check, FINDINGS A1). The count question stays indeterminate: a stored number (w1) or a count of the list (w2).
